title: Events & activities
text:
Earlier activities
In April 2024, I presented work on multivariate methods for understanding agricultural practices in cacao cultivation in the northern Ecuadorian Amazon, at ESPOL’s Showcase of Statistical Business Practice Projects in Guayaquil.
In October 2023, I helped organize the 20th Statistics Conference at ESPOL.

title: Research
text:
A stochastic process may depend on much more than its most recent state. In a process with infinite memory, the entire past can help determine what happens next. I’m interested in how to describe these processes mathematically and in what remains of that memory as time passes.
My current work centers on two related questions. First, when does a prescribed transition rule determine a unique probability law? Second, can processes started from different histories eventually lose the influence of those histories? The first concerns compatibility and uniqueness; the second leads to dynamic uniqueness.
I study these questions for chains with complete connections and \(g\)-measures on standard Borel spaces. Hellinger distances provide a way to compare probability laws, while absolute continuity and ergodic ideas help connect local transition rules with behavior on the entire future. Thinking of the shift as a measurable dynamical system is another useful perspective on the same problem.



Probability theory and stochastic processes, particularly processes with infinite memory.
Ergodic theory and measurable dynamical systems.
Stochastic differential equations and stochastic partial differential equations.

The first two areas are central to my current work. My interest in stochastic differential equations extends beyond that project and connects with earlier work in spatial statistics.
I’ll present a poster on this research at the 3rd Workshop on Combinatorics, Number Theory and Dynamical Systems in October 2026.

title: Research
text:
Earlier work
My background in statistics has also led me to problems where mathematical models and computation meet.

Spatial models and computation
At ESPOL, I developed SPDECensSpatial, an R implementation for spatial models with censored or missing responses. The work uses the SPDE representation of Matérn Gaussian random fields and sparse Gaussian Markov random fields to make inference and prediction computationally manageable. I implemented maximum-likelihood inference using the SAEM algorithm, along with uncertainty estimates and spatial prediction.
I also implemented the Independent Doubly Adaptive Rejection Metropolis Sampling (IA2RMS) algorithm in R, including its use within Gibbs sampling schemes.


Selective inference
I worked on inference after variable selection and outlier detection in robust regression. Conditioning on those decisions leads to truncated Gaussian distributions; my work included numerical procedures for finding the relevant truncation sets and computing selective \(p\)-values.


Multivariate methods
Another project explored agricultural practices among small-scale farmers in the northern Ecuadorian Amazon. I worked with dimensionality-reduction and projection methods, particularly t-SNE, to represent and examine multivariate data.

title: Pablo Zúñiga
text:
I’m Pablo, from Ecuador, and I now live in Campinas, Brazil. I came to mathematics through statistics, and my studies have gradually drawn me toward probability theory and more abstract mathematical questions. I’m currently pursuing a Master’s in Statistics at the University of Campinas (UNICAMP).
What I enjoy most about research is following a question far enough to understand the ideas behind it. These days, that often means thinking about randomness, memory, and the structures that govern a stochastic process.
I also care about communicating science: explaining why a question is worth asking, what research helps us understand, and how fundamental research can contribute to technology and society. I enjoy football and music, too.

title: Teaching
text:
In 2026, I’m a teaching assistant for ME414 — Statistics for Experimentalists at IMECC, UNICAMP, through the university’s Teaching Internship Program (PED). My teaching periods are March–June and August–December.
I help students work through probability distributions, estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, and analysis of variance. Alongside regular office hours, I’ve delivered selected lectures and guided problem-solving sessions on statistical inference.

title: A poster in Fortaleza
text:
I’ll be taking part in the 3rd Workshop on Combinatorics, Number Theory and Dynamical Systems, in Fortaleza, Brazil, from 19 to 23 October 2026.
My accepted poster, Hellinger Criteria for Uniqueness and Dynamic Uniqueness in Infinite-Memory Shift Systems, presents my current research on how dependence on the past affects the uniqueness of probability laws and the long-term behavior of stochastic processes.
The workshop takes place at Labomar — Instituto de Ciências do Mar, Universidade Federal do Ceará (UFC). The organizers have awarded me financial support to attend.
